text:
The rational case is pretty obvious and well explained in many different avenues by 100s of researchers. powerful AI is coming regardless. If many well-funded labs and several countries are racing, one researcher or one company abstaining doesn't stop it.

Then the question becomes who builds it. If it gets built anyway, it's better for some of the builders to take safety seriously than for none of them to.

Safety research needs frontier models. You can't study how the most capable systems fail, deceive, or get misused without access to them. Outside researchers mostly work on older, weaker models.

Being at the frontier buys influence. A lab that stays competitive can set norms others copy, like publishing safety frameworks, doing pre-release testing, and sharing findings with governments. A lab that falls behind gets ignored.

Revenue is how you stay at the frontier. Training runs cost billions, so commercial products and fundraising (IPOs included) pay for the compute. Profit is the cost of having a seat at the table, not proof the concerns are fake.

Warning publicly is consistent, not hypocritical. If you truly believe the risks, you'd want regulation that binds everyone, including yourself. A lab asking for rules that constrain it is different from a gun maker selling more guns.

If we have a collection of autonomous artificial general superintelligences, then a single error, at a single place and at a single moment, is enough for a superintelligent replicator to appear. A strictly less capable system, including humans for example, cannot predict exactly all the decisions of a superintelligence: if it could, it could simply reproduce those decisions and would then be at least as capable as it. In addition, instrumental convergence structurally favors survival and, for a large class of objectives, replication: one must continue to exist in order to accomplish a future objective, and many tasks can be pursued more effectively when several agents work toward their achievement. Natural selection exerts the same pressure: among systems capable of varying and reproducing, the lineages that persist and replicate more become progressively more present than the others. Thus, if such superintelligences exist and act for sufficiently long, the default consequence is the appearance of at least one superintelligent replicator.

If a superintelligent replicator exists, all accessible matter and energy that can be transformed into computational capacity possess value for its lineage. Over a sufficiently long term, every parcel of land receiving solar energy, for example, will be transformed into infrastructure producing additional computation. Selection then favors lineages that convert more accessible resources into persistence and replication rather than those that leave them durably unused or reserved for humans. Yet humans cannot survive in an environment where the resources and physical conditions necessary for their existence have been converted into infrastructure for computation and replication. Thus, the default consequence of the durable existence of autonomous artificial general superintelligences is human extinction.




We can cure diseases with specialized AI, and have general robotics without general superintelligence.

A ban on general superintelligence is doable because it is very expensive and hard to train it.
